at hade.explanation: "At hade" means "to hate", and it is a strong word. For everyday dislikes Danes often say something milder, like "Jeg kan ikke lide" (I don't like). "Jeg hader at vente" means "I hate waiting".

sentence.da: Man skal ikke **hade** andre, men elske dem.
sentence.en: You should not hate others, but love them.

at handle.explanation: "At handle" means "to shop", and also "to act". "Jeg handler i supermarkedet" means "I shop at the supermarket", and "at handle ind" means "to do the grocery shopping". With "om" (about) it means to be about something: "Filmen handler om kærlighed" (The film is about love).

sentence.da: Jeg skal **handle** i supermarkedet, for vi har ingen mælk.
sentence.en: I have to shop at the supermarket, because we have no milk.

at have.explanation: "At have" means "to have" or "to own". It is also used to say what you have done: "Jeg har spist" (I have eaten). Danish says "Jeg har fødselsdag" (I have birthday) where English says "It is my birthday".

sentence.da: Det er dejligt at **have** en bror og to søstre.
sentence.en: It is lovely to have a brother and two sisters.

at have brug for.explanation: "At have brug for" means "to need": "Jeg har brug for hjælp" (I need help). Literally it is "to have use for". "At behøve" (to need) is also common, especially in "du behøver ikke" (you do not need to).

sentence.da: Du kan **have brug for** en paraply, når det regner.
sentence.en: You may need an umbrella when it rains.

at have fødselsdag.explanation: "At have fødselsdag" means "to have a birthday", as in today is your birthday: "Jeg har fødselsdag i dag" (It is my birthday today). To congratulate someone, say "Tillykke med fødselsdagen!" (Happy birthday!).

sentence.da: Min bror skal **have fødselsdag** i morgen, så vi bager en kage.
sentence.en: My brother is having a birthday tomorrow, so we are baking a cake.

forms.en: I have had a pain in

at have ondt i.explanation: "At have ondt i" means "to have a pain in", and you use it to say a body part hurts. Put the body part after it: "Jeg har ondt i hovedet" (I have a headache) or "ondt i maven" (a stomach ache). Danish says "the head" where English says "my head".

sentence.da: Hvis du spiser ti kager, kan du **have ondt i** maven.
sentence.en: If you eat ten cakes, you can have a stomach ache.

at have på.explanation: "At have på" means "to wear", literally "to have on": "Hvad har du på?" (What are you wearing?). Putting clothes on is a different phrase, "at tage tøj på" (literally "take clothes on"), and taking them off is "at tage tøj af".

sentence.da: Du skal **have på** en varm jakke, for det er koldt.
sentence.en: You have to wear a warm jacket, because it is cold.

at have ret.explanation: "At have ret" means "to be right", but Danish literally says "to have right": "Du har ret" means "You are right". Do not use "er" (am) here.

sentence.da: Hvis du siger, at to plus to er fire, vil du **have ret**.
sentence.en: If you say that two plus two is four, you will be right.

at have travlt.explanation: "At have travlt" means "to be busy" or "to be in a hurry". Danish uses "have" (have) where English uses "be": "Jeg har travlt" is literally "I have busy".

sentence.da: Hvis toget går om to minutter, vil du **have travlt**.
sentence.en: If the train leaves in two minutes, you will be in a hurry.

at hedde.explanation: "At hedde" means "to be called", and it is how you give your name: "Jeg hedder Anna" means "My name is Anna". It is also used for things: "Hvad hedder det på dansk?" (What is that called in Danish?).

sentence.da: Vi får en lille pige, og hun skal **hedde** Anna.
sentence.en: We are having a little girl, and she will be called Anna.

at hente.explanation: "At hente" means "to fetch" or "to pick up", like collecting a person or a thing. "Jeg henter børnene i skolen" means "I pick up the children at school". "Kan du hente en kop kaffe?" means "Can you get a cup of coffee?".

sentence.da: Jeg skal **hente** børnene i skolen klokken tre.
sentence.en: I have to pick up the children at school at three o'clock.

at hjælpe.explanation: "At hjælpe" means "to help". You help someone directly, with no extra word: "Kan jeg hjælpe dig?" (Can I help you?). "Hjælp!" is also what you shout in an emergency.

sentence.da: Du har mange tasker, så jeg vil **hjælpe** dig.
sentence.en: You have many bags, so I will help you.

at hjælpe med.explanation: "At hjælpe med" means "to help with" something. After "med" (with) comes the task: "hjælpe med lektierne" (help with the homework). To say who you help, put the person right after "hjælper": "Jeg hjælper dig med maden" (I help you with the food).

sentence.da: Du har travlt, så jeg vil **hjælpe med** maden.
sentence.en: You are busy, so I will help with the food.

at holde.explanation: "At holde" means "to hold / keep". "Hold min taske" means "Hold my bag". It is also used in common phrases: "holde en fest" (to throw a party), "holde af" (to be fond of) and "holde pause" (to take a break).

sentence.da: Kan du **holde** min taske et øjeblik?
sentence.en: Can you hold my bag for a moment?

at hoppe.explanation: "At hoppe" means "to jump", for example into water, over a puddle or on a trampoline. Add a small word to show the direction: "hoppe op" (jump up), "hoppe ned" (jump down) and "hoppe i" (jump in).

sentence.da: Børnene vil **hoppe** i vandet, fordi det er varmt.
sentence.en: The children want to jump into the water because it is warm.

at hoste.explanation: "At hoste" means "to cough". "Jeg hoster meget" means "I cough a lot". For a cough that lasts, use the perfect: "Jeg har hostet i tre dage" (I have been coughing for three days).

sentence.da: Jeg er syg og må **hoste** hele natten.
sentence.en: I am sick and have to cough all night.

at huske.explanation: "At huske" means "to remember", both to recall something and to remember to do something. "Husk at ringe" means "Remember to call", and "Husk!" on its own means "Remember!". "At huske på" means "to keep in mind".

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke **huske** hans navn.
sentence.en: I can't remember his name.

at håbe.explanation: "At håbe" means "to hope": "Jeg håber, det går godt" (I hope it goes well). It is also a polite opener: "Jeg håber, du har det godt" (I hope you are well).

sentence.da: Vi må **håbe**, at det ikke regner i morgen.
sentence.en: We must hope that it does not rain tomorrow.

at høre.explanation: "At høre" means "to hear": "Jeg hører en lyd" (I hear a sound). It is also used for getting news: "Jeg har hørt, at han flytter" (I have heard that he is moving). For listening on purpose, use "at lytte" (to listen).

sentence.da: Jeg kan ikke **høre** dig.
sentence.en: I can't hear you.

en hals.explanation: "En hals" means both "a neck" and "a throat", because Danish has one word for both. "Jeg har ondt i halsen" means "I have a sore throat". A necklace is "en halskæde" (a neck chain).

sentence.da: Hun har en smuk kæde om sin **hals**.
sentence.en: She has a pretty chain around her neck.

en halv time.explanation: "En halv time" means "half an hour", or 30 minutes. Be careful with clock times: "halv fem" means 4:30, not 5:30, because Danes count the half hour toward the next hour.

sentence.da: Bussen kommer om en **halv time**, altså om 30 minutter.
sentence.en: The bus comes in half an hour, that is, in 30 minutes.

en handske.explanation: "En handske" means "a glove". Gloves come in pairs, so you mostly hear the plural "handsker" (gloves). The word contains "hånd" (hand).

sentence.da: Jeg har mistet en **handske**, så min venstre hånd er kold.
sentence.en: I have lost a glove, so my left hand is cold.

en hat.explanation: "En hat" means "a hat", usually one with a brim, like a sun hat. It is not the same as "en hue" (a warm knitted cap) or "en kasket" (a cap with a peak).

sentence.da: Solen skinner, så hun har en stor **hat** på hovedet.
sentence.en: The sun is shining, so she has a big hat on her head.

en have.explanation: "En have" means "a garden". Do not mix it up with "at have" (to have), which is spelled the same. "I haven" means "in the garden".

sentence.da: Vi har en **have** med blomster og træer.
sentence.en: We have a garden with flowers and trees.

en hest.explanation: "En hest" means "a horse". "At ride på hest" means "to go horse riding", using "at ride" (to ride). A small horse is "en pony" (a pony).

sentence.da: En **hest** har fire ben, og man kan ride på den.
sentence.en: A horse has four legs, and you can ride on it.

en himmel.explanation: "En himmel" means "a sky", and it can also mean "heaven". Danes mostly say "himlen" (the sky) for the sky. "Himlen er grå" means "The sky is grey".

sentence.da: Om natten er der en mørk **himmel** med mange stjerner.
sentence.en: At night there is a dark sky with many stars.

en historie.explanation: "En historie" means both "a story" and "history" (the past, also the school subject), and the situation shows which. "Fortæl en historie" means "tell a story", and "Danmarks historie" means "the history of Denmark".

sentence.da: Han fortæller en sjov **historie**.
sentence.en: He tells a funny story.

en hjemmesko.explanation: "En hjemmesko" means "a slipper". It is built from "hjemme" (at home) and "sko" (shoe), so it is literally a "home shoe". "At tage ... på" means "to put on": "Tag dine hjemmesko på" is "Put your slippers on".

sentence.da: Jeg tager mine **hjemmesko** på, når jeg kommer hjem.
sentence.en: I put my slippers on when I get home.

en hobby.explanation: "En hobby" means "a hobby", something you like to do in your free time. You can ask "Hvad er din hobby?" (What is your hobby?) or say "Jeg har mange hobbyer" (I have many hobbies).

sentence.da: Min **hobby** er at male billeder i min fritid.
sentence.en: My hobby is painting pictures in my free time.

en hoste.explanation: "En hoste" means "a cough". The same word is also the action: "at hoste" means "to cough". You can say "Jeg har en hoste" or "Jeg har hoste", both meaning "I have a cough".

sentence.da: Jeg har en slem **hoste**, og jeg hoster hele natten.
sentence.en: I have a bad cough, and I cough all night.

en hovedbanegård.explanation: "En hovedbanegård" means "a central station", the main train station of a big city. It is built from "hoved" (main), "bane" (railway) and "gård" (yard).

sentence.da: København har en stor **hovedbanegård**, hvor mange tog kommer og kører.
sentence.en: Copenhagen has a big central station where many trains come and go.

en hovedpine.explanation: "En hovedpine" means "a headache". It is built from "hoved" (head) and "pine" (pain). Danes say "Jeg har hovedpine" (I have a headache) without "en". "Jeg har ondt i hovedet" means the same, literally "I have a pain in the head".

sentence.da: Jeg har **hovedpine**, så jeg tager en pille.
sentence.en: I have a headache, so I am taking a pill.

en hovedret.explanation: "En hovedret" means "a main course". It is built from "hoved" (main) and "ret" (dish). You can ask "Hvad skal du have til hovedret?" (What are you having for the main course?).

sentence.da: Til forret tager jeg suppe, og til **hovedret** tager jeg fisk.
sentence.en: For the starter I have soup, and for the main course I have fish.

en hue.explanation: "En hue" means "a beanie", a knitted or woollen cap that keeps your head warm. It is different from "en hat" (a hat with a brim) and "en kasket" (a cap with a peak).

sentence.da: Det er koldt, så jeg har en varm **hue** på hovedet.
sentence.en: It is cold, so I have a warm beanie on my head.

en hund.explanation: "En hund" means "a dog". Danes say "Jeg går tur med hunden" for "I take the dog for a walk".

sentence.da: Min **hund** gør højt og løber efter katten.
sentence.en: My dog barks loudly and runs after the cat.

en hvidvin.explanation: "En hvidvin" means "a white wine". It is built from "hvid" (white) and "vin" (wine). Danish has no word for "of" here: "et glas hvidvin" means "a glass of white wine".

sentence.da: Jeg drikker et glas **hvidvin** til fisken, og min mand drikker rødvin.
sentence.en: I drink a glass of white wine with the fish, and my husband drinks red wine.

en hånd.explanation: "En hånd" means "a hand". "Vask dine hænder" means "Wash your hands". To shake hands, Danes say "at give hånd" (literally "to give hand").

sentence.da: Jeg har fem fingre på hver **hånd**.
sentence.en: I have five fingers on each hand.

en hæl.explanation: "En hæl" means "a heel", the back part of your foot, and also the raised back part of a shoe. "Sko med høje hæle" means "shoes with high heels".

sentence.da: Jeg har ondt bag på foden, i min **hæl**.
sentence.en: I have a pain at the back of the foot, in my heel.

en hæveautomat.explanation: "En hæveautomat" means "an ATM", a machine where you take out cash. It comes from "at hæve" (to withdraw) and "automat" (machine), so "at hæve penge" means "to withdraw money".

sentence.da: Jeg har ingen kontanter, så jeg leder efter en **hæveautomat**.
sentence.en: I have no cash, so I am looking for an ATM.

et hav.explanation: "Et hav" means "a sea" or "an ocean", a very large area of salt water. "Ved havet" means "by the sea" and "ud på havet" means "out at sea".

sentence.da: Skibet sejler over det store **hav**.
sentence.en: The ship sails across the big sea.

et hjem.explanation: "Et hjem" means "a home", the place where you live and feel at home, not just the building (that is "et hus", a house). "Hjemme" means "at home" and "hjem" alone means "toward home": "Jeg går hjem" is "I am going home".

sentence.da: Jeg er langt fra mit **hjem** og savner min familie.
sentence.en: I am far from my home and miss my family.

et hjerte.explanation: "Et hjerte" means "a heart". The "h" is silent, so the word starts like the "y" in English "yes". It is used for the body part and for feelings: "med hele mit hjerte" means "with all my heart".

sentence.da: Mit **hjerte** slår hurtigt.
sentence.en: My heart is beating fast.

et hospital.explanation: "Et hospital" means "a hospital". "På hospitalet" means "at the hospital". Danes also say "et sygehus" (literally "a sick house") for a hospital.

sentence.da: Min mor er syg, så hun ligger på et **hospital**.
sentence.en: My mother is sick, so she is in a hospital.

et hotel.explanation: "Et hotel" means "a hotel". "På hotellet" means "at the hotel". To say you are staying at one, Danes say "Vi bor på hotel" (We are staying at a hotel).

sentence.da: Vi sover to nætter på et **hotel** i København.
sentence.en: We sleep two nights in a hotel in Copenhagen.

et hotelværelse.explanation: "Et hotelværelse" means "a hotel room". It is made of "et hotel" (a hotel) and "et værelse" (a room). "Værelse" alone can mean any room you sleep in or rent.

sentence.da: Mit **hotelværelse** har udsigt til havnen.
sentence.en: My hotel room has a view of the harbour.

et hoved.explanation: "Et hoved" means "a head". Danish says "the head" where English says "my head": "Jeg har ondt i hovedet" is literally "I have a pain in the head" and means "my head hurts". It is also in "hovedpine" (headache) and "hovedstad" (capital city).

sentence.da: Hun har en stor hat på sit **hoved**.
sentence.en: She has a big hat on her head.

et hus.explanation: "Et hus" means "a house", the building where people live. Do not mix it up with "et hjem" (a home), which is about the place where you feel at home rather than the building.

sentence.da: Vi bor i et stort **hus** med en have og et rødt tag.
sentence.en: We live in a big house with a garden and a red roof.

hallo.explanation: "Hallo" means "hello". Danes use it when answering the phone and when calling out to get someone's attention. For greeting someone face to face they prefer "hej" (hi). Said sharply, "hallo!" can mean "hey, listen!".

sentence.da: Telefonen ringer. **Hallo**, hvem er det?
sentence.en: The phone rings. Hello, who is it?

halv.explanation: "Halv" means "half": "en halv pizza" (half a pizza), "en halv time" (half an hour). With the clock it works differently from English: "klokken fire" is 4:00, but "halv fire" is 3:30, half an hour before four, not after three.

sentence.da: Jeg spiser ikke en hel pizza, kun en **halv** pizza.
sentence.en: I am not eating a whole pizza, only half a pizza.

forms.en: See you at half past six.

halv tre.explanation: "Halv tre" means "half past two", not half past three. Danes count half way toward the next hour, so 2:30 is "halv tre" (half way to three) and 6:30 is "halv syv" (half way to seven).

sentence.da: Vi mødes **halv tre**, en halv time før klokken tre.
sentence.en: We meet at half past two, half an hour before three o'clock.

halvdelen.explanation: "Halvdelen" means "the half (of it)". You usually say what it is half of with "af" (of): "halvdelen af kagen" (half of the cake). To say just "half a ..." use "halv" (half), as in "en halv liter" (half a liter).

sentence.da: Jeg har spist **halvdelen** af kagen.
sentence.en: I have eaten half of the cake.

halvfems.explanation: "Halvfems" means "ninety". Danes count it as "half way to five twenties" (4½ x 20 = 90). Compare "firs" (80, four twenties) with "halvfems" (90). For 91, the ones come first: "enoghalvfems" is literally "one-and-ninety".

sentence.da: Min bedstefar er **halvfems** år og snart hundrede.
sentence.en: My grandfather is ninety years old and soon a hundred.

halvfjerds.explanation: "Halvfjerds" means "seventy". Danes count it as "half way to four twenties" (3½ x 20 = 70). For 71, the ones come first: "enoghalvfjerds" is literally "one-and-seventy".

sentence.da: Jeg er tres, og min mor er ti år ældre, **halvfjerds**.
sentence.en: I am sixty, and my mother is ten years older, seventy.

halvtreds.explanation: "Halvtreds" means "fifty". Danes count it as "half way to three twenties" (2½ x 20 = 50). "En kaffe koster halvtreds kroner" means "A coffee costs fifty kroner".

sentence.da: Jeg har hundrede kroner og giver dig halvdelen, **halvtreds** kroner.
sentence.en: I have a hundred kroner and give you half, fifty kroner.

ham.explanation: "Ham" means "him". Compare "Han hjælper mig" (He helps me) with "Jeg hjælper ham" (I help him): "han" is the man who helps, "ham" is the man who gets the help. It is also used after words like "til" (to) and "med" (with): "Giv det til ham" (Give it to him). "Hans" is a different word, meaning "his".

sentence.da: Peter er min ven, og jeg kan lide **ham**.
sentence.en: Peter is my friend, and I like him.

han.explanation: "Han" means "he". Compare "Han hjælper mig" (He helps me) with "Jeg hjælper ham" (I help him): "han" is the man who helps, "ham" is the man who gets the help. "Hans" means "his": "hans bil" (his car).

sentence.da: Peter er min bror, og **han** er lærer.
sentence.en: Peter is my brother, and he is a teacher.

handsker.explanation: "Handsker" means "gloves", and one glove is "en handske". Gloves come in pairs, so "et par handsker" means "a pair of gloves". The word is built from "hånd" (hand). Mittens are "vanter".

sentence.da: Mine hænder er kolde, så jeg tager **handsker** på.
sentence.en: My hands are cold, so I put gloves on.

hans.explanation: "Hans" means "his". "Han har en bil. Det er hans bil" (He has a car. It is his car). It never changes: "hans bil" (his car), "hans hus" (his house), "hans børn" (his children). Compare "Peter vasker hans bil" (Peter washes some other man's car) with "Peter vasker sin bil" (Peter washes his own car).

sentence.da: Peter har en bil, og **hans** bil er rød.
sentence.en: Peter has a car, and his car is red.

hav en god dag.explanation: "Hav en god dag" means "have a good day" and is a friendly goodbye in shops and offices. You can swap "dag" (day) for "aften" (evening) or "weekend". The usual reply is "i lige måde" (same to you).

sentence.da: Tak for hjælpen. **Hav en god dag!**
sentence.en: Thanks for the help. Have a good day!

hej.explanation: "Hej" means "hi" or "hello" and is used with almost everyone, friends and strangers, young and old. It is also used when you leave, often as "hej hej" (bye bye). It sounds a lot like the English "hi".

sentence.da: **Hej**, jeg hedder Anna.
sentence.en: Hi, my name is Anna.

hej med dig.explanation: "Hej med dig" means "hi there" when you meet and "bye" when you part, so the meaning depends on the moment. For several people say "hej med jer" (hi to you all). "Hej hej" (said twice) is mostly used for goodbye.

sentence.da: **Hej med dig**, hvordan går det?
sentence.en: Hi there, how is it going?

hejsa.explanation: "Hejsa" means "hi there" or "hey". It is a cheerful, informal version of "hej" (hi). Use it with friends, family and children, not in formal situations, where "goddag" (good day) is better. "Hej hej" is more often used for goodbye.

sentence.da: **Hejsa**, hvad laver du?
sentence.en: Hi there, what are you doing?

helbred.explanation: "Helbred" means "health", meaning how well your body is doing. It is used for the state of your body: "Pas på dit helbred" (Take care of your health).

sentence.da: Min bedstefar er gammel, men han har et godt **helbred** og er aldrig syg.
sentence.en: My grandfather is old, but he has good health and is never sick.

held og lykke.explanation: "Held og lykke" means "good luck" and literally "luck and happiness". It is the normal way to wish someone luck before an exam, interview or new start. Add "med" (with) and what it is about: "held og lykke med prøven" (good luck with the test).

sentence.da: **Held og lykke** med dit nye job!
sentence.en: Good luck with your new job!

heldig.explanation: "Heldig" means "lucky". It comes from "held" (luck). From it you also get "heldigvis" (luckily): "Heldigvis regner det ikke" (Luckily it is not raining).

sentence.da: Du fandt hundrede kroner på gaden. Du er **heldig**!
sentence.en: You found a hundred kroner on the street. You are lucky!

hele tiden.explanation: "Hele tiden" means "all the time". It is literally "the whole time", with no break: "Han taler hele tiden" (He talks all the time), "Det regner hele tiden" (It rains all the time). It often sounds like a complaint.

sentence.da: Min telefon ringer **hele tiden**, og det er irriterende.
sentence.en: My phone rings all the time, and that is annoying.

heller.explanation: "Heller" means "either", as in "can't ... either". Compare "Jeg kan også komme" (I can come too) with "Jeg kan heller ikke komme" (I can't come either). "Heller" always goes with a no-word like "ikke" (not): "heller ikke i dag" (not today either).

sentence.da: Anna kan ikke komme, og jeg kan **heller** ikke komme.
sentence.en: Anna can't come, and I can't come either.

forms.da: hellere i dag end i morgen

hellere.explanation: "Hellere" means "rather". It says what you would choose instead: "Jeg vil hellere have te" (I would rather have tea), "Du må hellere gå" (You had better go). Do not mix it up with "heller" in "heller ikke" (not ... either).

sentence.da: Jeg vil **hellere** have te end kaffe.
sentence.en: I would rather have tea than coffee.

helst.explanation: "Helst" means "preferably" or "most of all". It shows your first choice: "Jeg vil helst have te" (I would most like tea), "Hvad vil du helst?" (What would you like most?). "Helst ikke" is a soft no: "Skal du med?" - "Helst ikke" (Are you coming? - Preferably not).

sentence.da: Jeg kan gå i biografen, men jeg vil **helst** blive hjemme.
sentence.en: I could go to the cinema, but I would most like to stay at home.

helt.explanation: "Helt" means "completely". It makes the next word stronger. Compare "Jeg er enig" (I agree) with "Jeg er helt enig" (I completely agree), and "næsten færdig" (almost done) with "helt færdig" (completely done).

sentence.da: Jeg er **helt** enig med dig.
sentence.en: I completely agree with you.

hende.explanation: "Hende" means "her". Compare "Hun hjælper mig" (She helps me) with "Jeg hjælper hende" (I help her): "hun" is the woman who helps, "hende" is the woman who gets the help. It is also used after words like "til" (to): "Giv det til hende" (Give it to her). "Hendes" is a different word: "hendes bil" (her car).

sentence.da: Anna er sød, og jeg kan lide **hende**.
sentence.en: Anna is nice, and I like her.

hendes.explanation: "Hendes" means "her" or "hers", for something that belongs to a woman or girl: "Anna har en taske. Det er hendes taske" (Anna has a bag. It is her bag). It never changes: "hendes bil", "hendes børn" (her car, her children). Compare "Anna vasker hendes bil" (Anna washes some other woman's car) with "Anna vasker sin bil" (Anna washes her own car).

sentence.da: Anna har en taske, og **hendes** taske er blå.
sentence.en: Anna has a bag, and her bag is blue.

her.explanation: "Her" means "here", the place where you are. Compare "Jeg står her" (I am standing here) with "Du står der" (You are standing there). Careful: it looks like English "her", but that is "hende" in Danish. In everyday speech "den her bog" means "this book".

sentence.da: Du står der, og jeg står **her**.
sentence.en: You are standing there, and I am standing here.

herinde.explanation: "Herinde" means "in here". You say it when you are inside the place yourself: "Jeg er herinde i køkkenet" (I am in here in the kitchen). Someone outside says "derinde" (in there): "Hun er derinde" (She is in there). To move inside, use "ind": "Kom ind!" (Come in!).

sentence.da: Det er koldt udenfor, men varmt **herinde**.
sentence.en: It is cold outside, but warm in here.

hinanden.explanation: "Hinanden" means "each other". Compare "Anna hjælper Peter" (Anna helps Peter) with "De hjælper hinanden" (They help each other). It also fits "se på hinanden" (look at each other) and "snakke med hinanden" (talk to each other). Compare "De vasker sig" (They wash themselves) with "De vasker hinanden" (They wash each other).

sentence.da: Anna hjælper Peter, og Peter hjælper Anna. De hjælper **hinanden**.
sentence.en: Anna helps Peter, and Peter helps Anna. They help each other.

hjem.explanation: "Hjem" means "home" when you are heading there. Compare "Jeg går hjem" (I am going home) with "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home). "Hjem" goes with words for moving, like "gå" (go), "køre" (drive) and "komme" (come).

sentence.da: Arbejdet er slut, og jeg skal **hjem** nu.
sentence.en: Work is over, and I am going home now.

hjemme.explanation: "Hjemme" means "at home", where you already are. Compare "Jeg er hjemme" (I am at home) with "Jeg går hjem" (I am going home). "Hjemme hos mig" means "at my place".

sentence.da: Jeg går ikke ud i aften, jeg er **hjemme**.
sentence.en: I am not going out tonight, I am at home.

hjælp.explanation: "Hjælp" means "help", and it is usually used without "en" in front, as in "Jeg har brug for hjælp" (I need help). It is also what you shout in an emergency: "Hjælp!".

sentence.da: Min bil vil ikke starte. Jeg har brug for **hjælp**!
sentence.en: My car won't start. I need help!

holland.explanation: "Holland" means "the Netherlands". Danish uses no "the" with it: "i Holland" is "in the Netherlands". Danes say "Holland" for the whole country, though the formal name is "Nederlandene".

sentence.da: I **Holland** taler de hollandsk.
sentence.en: In the Netherlands they speak Dutch.

hollandsk.explanation: "Hollandsk" means "Dutch", both for things from the Netherlands and for the language. Danish writes it with a small first letter, even though "Dutch" has a capital in English.

sentence.da: Han bor i Holland og taler **hollandsk**.
sentence.en: He lives in the Netherlands and speaks Dutch.

honning.explanation: "Honning" means "honey". You cannot count it, so it is usually said without "en" in front, as in "lidt honning" (a little honey).

sentence.da: Jeg tager lidt **honning** i teen, så den bliver sød.
sentence.en: I put a little honey in the tea so that it gets sweet.

hos.explanation: "Hos" means "at someone's place", and a person comes after it: "hos min ven" (at my friend's place), "hos lægen" (at the doctor's). For a building or place, use "på" or "i": "på biblioteket" (at the library), "i køkkenet" (in the kitchen). Compare "Jeg er hos lægen" (I am at the doctor's) with "Jeg er på hospitalet" (I am at the hospital).

sentence.da: Jeg sover **hos** min ven i nat.
sentence.en: I am sleeping at my friend's place tonight.

hud.explanation: "En hud" means "a skin", but Danes mostly just say "hud" for the skin on your body: "Min hud er tør" (My skin is dry). You will also see it in "hudcreme" (skin cream).

sentence.da: Jeg bruger creme, fordi min **hud** er meget tør.
sentence.en: I use cream because my skin is very dry.

hun.explanation: "Hun" means "she". Compare "Hun hjælper mig" (She helps me) with "Jeg hjælper hende" (I help her): "hun" is the woman who helps, "hende" is the woman who gets the help. In questions it stays "hun": "Er hun hjemme?" (Is she at home?).

sentence.da: Anna er min søster, og **hun** er lærer.
sentence.en: Anna is my sister, and she is a teacher.

hundrede.explanation: "Hundrede" means "hundred". It stays the same after other numbers: "to hundrede" (200) and "tre hundrede" (300). For 100 you can just say "hundrede", with no "one" in front.

sentence.da: Ti gange ti er **hundrede**.
sentence.en: Ten times ten is a hundred.

hurtig.explanation: "Hurtig" means "fast" or "quick", for people, cars, answers and actions. To say how someone does something, use "hurtigt" (quickly): "Han løber hurtigt" (He runs fast).

sentence.da: Cyklen er langsom, men bilen er **hurtig**.
sentence.en: The bicycle is slow, but the car is fast.

hvad.explanation: "Hvad" means "what" and asks about a thing: "Hvad er det?" (What is that?). For a person use "hvem": "Hvem er det?" (Who is that?). Said alone, "Hvad?" means "Pardon?", but it can sound blunt, so "Undskyld?" (Excuse me?) is more polite.

sentence.da: **Hvad** hedder du?
sentence.en: What is your name?

hvad betyder det?.explanation: "Hvad betyder det?" means "What does that mean?". To ask about one word, put it after "betyder" (means): "Hvad betyder 'hej'?" (What does "hej" mean?).

sentence.da: Jeg forstår ikke ordet. **Hvad betyder det?**
sentence.en: I don't understand the word. What does that mean?

hvad er klokken?.explanation: "Hvad er klokken?" means "What time is it?" Literally it asks "what is the clock?", because "klokken" means "the clock". You answer with "klokken er" (it is) plus the time. A polite alternative is "ved du, hvad klokken er?" (do you know what time it is?).

sentence.da: Undskyld, **hvad er klokken?**
sentence.en: Excuse me, what time is it?

forms.en: What is that called in Danish?
What is that called in English?

hvad hedder det på dansk?.explanation: "Hvad hedder det på dansk?" means "What is that called in Danish?". "Hedder" means "is called", the same word used for names: "jeg hedder Anna" (my name is Anna). Swap "dansk" (Danish) for another language, such as "engelsk" (English).

sentence.da: Det her hedder "dog" på engelsk. **Hvad hedder det på dansk?**
sentence.en: This is called "dog" in English. What is that called in Danish?

hvad hedder du?.explanation: "Hvad hedder du?" means "What's your name?" and literally "What are you called?". You answer "Jeg hedder Anna" (My name is Anna).

sentence.da: **Hvad hedder du?** - Jeg hedder Anna.
sentence.en: What's your name? - My name is Anna.

hvad koster det?.explanation: "Hvad koster det?" means "How much does it cost?". Say "det" for things like "et hus" (a house) and "den" for things like "en bog" (a book): "hvad koster den?" For several things say "hvad koster de?" (how much are they?).

sentence.da: **Hvad koster det?** Jeg vil gerne købe den.
sentence.en: How much does it cost? I'd like to buy it.

forms.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

hvad laver du?.explanation: "Hvad laver du?" means "What are you doing?" and can mean right now or in general, like "what do you do?". To ask about someone's job, "hvad arbejder du med?" (what do you work with?) is clearer. With several people say "hvad laver I?" (what are you all doing?).

sentence.da: **Hvad laver du** i aften?
sentence.en: What are you doing tonight?

hvad med dig?.explanation: "Hvad med dig?" means "What about you?" and turns a question back to the other person. Use "hvad med jer?" (what about you all?) for several people. You can put anyone in place of "dig", for example "hvad med Anna?" (what about Anna?).

sentence.da: Jeg har det godt. **Hvad med dig?**
sentence.en: I'm doing well. What about you?

hvad så?.explanation: "Hvad så?" literally means "what then?" and is a casual greeting like "what's up?" or "how's it going?". Friends use it instead of "hvordan har du det?" (how are you?). Keep it mostly for friends and people you know well.

sentence.da: Hej Anna, **hvad så?**
sentence.en: Hi Anna, what's up?

hvem.explanation: "Hvem" means "who" and asks about a person. Compare "Hvad er det?" (What is that? - a thing) with "Hvem er det?" (Who is that? - a person). It also works after small words like "med" (with): "Med hvem skal du rejse?" (Who are you travelling with?).

sentence.da: **Hvem** er din lærer?
sentence.en: Who is your teacher?

hver.explanation: "Hver" means "each" or "every". Compare "hver dag" (every day) with "hvert år" (every year): "hver" goes with en-words like "dag", and "hvert" goes with et-words like "år". "Jeg løber hver morgen" means "I run every morning".

sentence.da: Jeg løber **hver** morgen.
sentence.en: I run every morning.

hver dag.explanation: "Hver dag" means "every day". "Hver" (each, every) goes with en-words like "dag" (day); with et-words it becomes "hvert", as in "hvert år" (every year).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker kaffe **hver dag**.
sentence.en: I drink coffee every day.

hvert.explanation: "Hvert" means "each" or "every" before et-words: "hvert år" (every year), "hvert hus" (each house). Before en-words use "hver" instead: "hver dag" (every day), "hver bil" (each car).

sentence.da: Vi rejser **hvert** år til Sverige.
sentence.en: We travel to Sweden every year.

hvid.explanation: "Hvid" means "white". The "h" at the start is silent, so the word starts with a "v" sound.

sentence.da: Sneen er kold og **hvid**.
sentence.en: The snow is cold and white.

hvidløg.explanation: "Hvidløg" means "garlic". It is made of "hvid" (white) and "løg" (onion), so it is literally "white onion". Garlic is counted in cloves: "to fed hvidløg" (two cloves of garlic).

sentence.da: **Hvidløg** er hvidt og lugter stærkt.
sentence.en: Garlic is white and smells strong.

hvilken.explanation: "Hvilken" means "which". Compare "Hvad vil du have?" (What do you want?) with "Hvilken bil vil du have?" (Which car do you want?): "hvad" stands alone, while "hvilken" comes right before the thing you are asking about. "Hvilket hus?" and "Hvilke bøger?" are in the forms above.

sentence.da: **Hvilken** farve kan du bedst lide?
sentence.en: Which colour do you like best?

hvis.explanation: "Hvis" means "if" and sets a condition: "Hvis det regner, bliver vi hjemme" (If it rains, we stay at home). Do not mix it up with "om" (whether), as in "Jeg ved ikke, om han kommer" (I don't know whether he is coming).

sentence.da: **Hvis** du er sulten, kan du spise med os.
sentence.en: If you are hungry, you can eat with us.

hvor.explanation: "Hvor" means "where": "Hvor bor du?" (Where do you live?). Before a word that describes, it means "how": "hvor gammel" (how old), "hvor meget" (how much), "hvor mange" (how many). "Hvor gammel er du?" means "How old are you?".

sentence.da: **Hvor** er min taske? Jeg kan ikke finde den.
sentence.en: Where is my bag? I can't find it.

hvor er toilettet?.explanation: "Hvor er toilettet?" means "Where is the restroom?" It is made of "hvor" (where), "er" (is) and "toilettet" (the toilet). Starting with "undskyld" (excuse me) makes it polite.

sentence.da: Undskyld, **hvor er toilettet?**
sentence.en: Excuse me, where is the restroom?

hvor gammel er du?.explanation: "Hvor gammel er du?" means "How old are you?" It is made of "hvor" (how), "gammel" (old), "er" (is) and "du" (you). In the answer you can leave out "gammel": "Jeg er tyve år" (I am twenty years old).

sentence.da: **Hvor gammel er du?** - Jeg er tyve år.
sentence.en: How old are you? - I am twenty years old.

forms.en: Where do you all come from?

hvor kommer du fra?.explanation: "Hvor kommer du fra?" means "Where are you from?" Literally it is "Where do you come from?" You answer "Jeg kommer fra England" (I come from England). As in English, "fra" (from) goes at the end of the question.

sentence.da: **Hvor kommer du fra?** - Jeg kommer fra England.
sentence.en: Where are you from? - I'm from England.

forms.en: How much does it cost? (for an en-word thing)

hvor meget koster det?.explanation: "Hvor meget koster det?" means "How much does it cost?" Word by word it is "how much costs it", with "hvor meget" (how much), "koster" (costs) and "det" (it).

sentence.da: Jeg vil købe brødet. **Hvor meget koster det?**
sentence.en: I want to buy the bread. How much does it cost?

hvordan.explanation: "Hvordan" means "how" and asks in what way something is done: "Hvordan laver man kaffe?" (How do you make coffee?). Before a word like old, much or many, Danish uses "hvor" instead: "Hvor gammel er du?" (How old are you?), "Hvor mange børn har du?" (How many children do you have?). "Hvordan går det?" means "How is it going?".

sentence.da: **Hvordan** kommer jeg til stationen?
sentence.en: How do I get to the station?

hvordan går det?.explanation: "Hvordan går det?" means "How's it going?" and is a common, casual way to ask how someone is. A normal answer is "Det går godt, tak" (It's going well, thanks), and you can ask back with "og dig?" (and you?).

sentence.da: **Hvordan går det?** - Det går godt, tak.
sentence.en: How's it going? - It's going well, thanks.

hvordan har du det?.explanation: "Hvordan har du det?" means "How are you?" Literally it is "how have you it". Answer with "Jeg har det godt" (I'm doing well) or "Fint, tak" (Fine, thanks).

sentence.da: Hej Peter! **Hvordan har du det?**
sentence.en: Hi Peter! How are you?

hvorfor.explanation: "Hvorfor" means "why" and asks for a reason. The answer often starts with "fordi" (because): "Hvorfor kommer du ikke?" - "Fordi jeg er syg." (Why aren't you coming? - Because I am sick.) "Hvorfor ikke?" means "Why not?".

sentence.da: **Hvorfor** er du så glad?
sentence.en: Why are you so happy?

hvornår.explanation: "Hvornår" means "when" in a question: "Hvornår kommer toget?" (When does the train come?). In the middle of a sentence, "when" is "når": "Jeg ringer, når jeg kommer hjem" (I will call when I get home). For one finished event in the past, use "da": "Jeg var glad, da du kom" (I was happy when you came).

related.en: when (in a sentence, repeated or in the future)

sentence.da: **Hvornår** åbner butikken?
sentence.en: When does the shop open?

hyggelig.explanation: "Hyggelig" means "cozy", "pleasant" or "nice" and describes a place, an evening or a person: "Han er hyggelig" means "He is nice to be around". It comes from "hygge" (a warm, relaxed, cozy feeling).

sentence.da: Det var en **hyggelig** aften med god mad og gode venner.
sentence.en: It was a cozy evening with good food and good friends.

hyggeligt at møde dig.explanation: "Hyggeligt at møde dig" means "nice to meet you" (literally "cozy to meet you"). Reply "I lige måde" (likewise). For someone you already know, say "hyggeligt at se dig" (nice to see you).

sentence.da: Jeg hedder Maja. **Hyggeligt at møde dig.**
sentence.en: I'm Maja. Nice to meet you.

håndbagage.explanation: "Håndbagage" means "carry-on luggage", the small bags you take with you into the plane cabin. It is made of "hånd" (hand) and "bagage" (luggage), so it is literally "hand luggage".

sentence.da: Jeg har ingen kuffert, kun **håndbagage** til flyet.
sentence.en: I have no suitcase, only carry-on luggage for the plane.

håndbold.explanation: "Håndbold" means "handball", the team sport. It is made of "hånd" (hand) and "bold" (ball). For the sport you leave out "en": "Jeg spiller håndbold" (I play handball). "En håndbold" is the ball itself.

sentence.da: Når man spiller **håndbold**, kaster man bolden i mål.
sentence.en: When you play handball, you throw the ball into the goal.

hår.explanation: "Hår" means "hair", all the hair on your head: "Hun har langt hår" (She has long hair). One single strand is "et hår" (a hair).

sentence.da: Hun har langt **hår**.
sentence.en: She has long hair.

hård.explanation: "Hård" means "hard" as in firm, not soft: "en hård seng" (a hard bed). It can also mean tough: "et hårdt job" (a tough job). For "hard" meaning "difficult", Danes usually say "svær" (difficult): "en svær opgave" (a difficult task).

sentence.da: Sengen er for **hård**, og jeg vil have en blød.
sentence.en: The bed is too hard, and I want a soft one.

høj.explanation: "Høj" means "tall" or "high", for people and for things. "Højt" also means "loudly": "Tal højt" means "Speak loudly".

sentence.da: Han er meget **høj** og kan nå det øverste skab.
sentence.en: He is very tall and can reach the top cupboard.

højre.explanation: "Højre" means "right", as in the right side or the right hand. For directions you say "til højre" (to the right): "Drej til højre" (Turn right).

sentence.da: Jeg skriver med min **højre** hånd.
sentence.en: I write with my right hand.
